description: Ông Địa is the earth god of the Vietnamese household, depicted as a jovial bald old man with a long beard who resides beneath the home, in gardens, or fields. He protects the family from misfortune and brings prosperity in exchange for offerings and reverence. His cult blends Buddhist practice with indigenous folk religion, and he is among the most widely honored domestic deities in Vietnam.
source: Vietnamese folklore, Lĩnh Nam chích quái
research_notes: Matches input appearance (bald bearded old man), behavior (protection, offerings), habitat (under houses, gardens, fields), and cultural significance. Vietnamese earth god, closely related to Thổ Công and Ông Táo traditions.

description: Nyai Roro Kidul is the goddess-queen of the Southern Ocean in Javanese and Sundanese belief, appearing as a beautiful woman in royal green robes with a spirit retinue. She rules the waters and is said to draw those who wear green into her undersea kingdom as soldiers. Revered across Java, she is the subject of widespread taboos: hotels, beaches, and courts forbid wearing green in her presence.
source: Indonesian folklore
research_notes: Matches input appearance, behavior (attracting people wearing green), habitat (Southern Ocean), and cultural significance (green-clothing taboo). Queen of the Southern Ocean, consort of the sultans of Mataram and Yogyakarta in court tradition.

description: Wewe Gombel is a ghost of Javanese folklore said to dwell in tall trees, bamboo groves, and abandoned wells, seizing neglected or disobedient children. Documented by the folklorist James Danandjaja, the figure acts as an instrument of moral education, warning children that misbehavior draws its attention. It relies on the didactic use of supernatural fear in Javanese child-rearing.
source: Indonesian mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections
research_notes: Matches input appearance, behavior (kidnapping naughty or neglected children), habitat, and cultural significance (documented by James Danandjaja; moral-education function).

Wolves are not native to Laos, and Lao animist cosmology centers on phi spirits, the protective khwan (thirty-two souls), and tiger- or dog-related shapeshifters (weretigers), with no wolf figure. The description appears to be a generic forest-spirit template applied without documentary basis.

description: Not attested in Mapuche mythology: the Mapuche trickster is the fox (ngürü), whose deceitful adventures fill a large cycle of tales, while no wolf-trickster figure exists. Mapuche tradition includes wekufe, harmful shapeshifting spirits, and the punalka, a wolf-like night creature, but neither functions as a trickster. The record also misplaces this South American figure in Myanmar.

Country field (Myanmar) is wrong. Flagged for removal or correction.

description: Barong is the protective spirit of Balinese tradition, a shaggy lion-dog deity usually portrayed by two dancers within an elaborate costume. In the celebrated Barong dance he confronts Rangda, the widow-witch, in ritual combat that stages the balance of cosmic order, blessing the village and warding off evil. The figure remains central to Balinese religious performance and community identity.
source: Indonesian folklore
research_notes: Matches input appearance (lion-dog worn by two dancers), behavior (protecting humans from Rangda, maintaining cosmic balance), habitat (Balinese villages), and cultural significance (Barong Dance).

description: Spirit helpers are the benevolent tutelary beings of Hmong shamanic tradition, assisting the shaman during trance journeys and aiding humans in daily tasks and healing. Each shaman relies on personal helping spirits (neeb) gained through initiation and maintained by offerings and respect. Documented in ethnographies of Hmong spirituality, they remain a functioning part of religious life.
source: Hmong shamanic tradition; spirit helper lore documented in ethnographies of Hmong spiritual practices
research_notes: Verified via ethnographies of Hmong shamanism (helping spirits/neeb). Input appearance/habitat were generic placeholders ('Unknown'); replaced with ethnographic content. Input living_tradition=False is doubtful — Hmong shamanism is actively practiced.

description: The oriole (vàng anh) is a spirit figure of Vietnamese folk narrative, most famously in the tale of Tấm and Cám, where the wronged heroine is transformed into an oriole that sings beside the royal palace and later into other natural forms. The oriole's transformations express themes of death, rebirth, and the eventual triumph of justice in Vietnamese storytelling.
source: Vietnamese folklore; oriole appears in folk tales and traditional Vietnamese literature
research_notes: The oriole (andng oanh) appears in the Tấm and Cám cycle, where Tấm becomes the bird after her murder; the bird is then killed by her stepsister, continuing the transformation chain. Matches the Vietnam setting of the input.

description: The rice spirit of Lao and Thai tradition, closely tied to Mae Phosop (Mother Rice), holds the life force believed to inhabit the rice crop. Farmers propitiate her with rituals and offerings at planting and harvest, and the loss of her presence is thought to drain fields of vitality. The figure links agricultural practice with animist cosmology in mainland Southeast Asia.
source: Laotian and Thai folklore; Mae Phosop and related rice spirit traditions of Southeast Asia
research_notes: Mae Phosop (Phosop) is the Thai-Lao rice goddess, well documented in agricultural ritual; the Lao khwan khao ('soul of rice') ceremony parallels it. Matches the Laos setting of the input.

description: The hamsa, known in Burmese as hintha, is a sacred water-bird, usually identified with the Brahminy duck, that occupies a central place in Mon and Burmese Buddhist mythology. It is the symbol of the Mon people and of the city of Pegu (Bago), and paired hintha images appear widely in temple art and architecture. In Buddhist contexts the hintha is auspicious and revered, not a demonic being.
source: Burmese folklore; the Hintha bird (Hamsa) appears in Mon and Burmese Buddhist mythology
research_notes: Input archetype 'demonic-entity' contradicts the hintha's sacred, auspicious status (symbol of Mon people and Bago). Input appearance/habitat were generic placeholders; corrected. Living_tradition=False in input is questionable given continued cultural use.

description: At the Hmong New Year (Noj Peb Caug) a ceremonial address honors Ntoo Xeeb, the titular spirit of the new year, together with four benevolent spirits of the locality. Recorded in an ethnography of the Ban Mae Sa Mai community in northern Thailand, the ceremony combines expiation, supplication, and sacrifice to renew the community's standing with the spirit world at the turn of the year.
source: Hmong folklore; New Year spirit traditions from Hmong cultural and shamanic practices (cf. J. Heisig, 'The Hmong New Year Ceremony', Asian Ethnology)

description: Tāne is the Polynesian god of forests and birds, best known in Māori tradition as Tāne Mahuta, who separated earth and sky and gave humanity the trees of the forest. The record identifies him as a Tahitian forest deity honored through carved wooden figures in temples. Note that the figure belongs to Polynesian, not French, tradition despite the country tag on this record.

description: El Trasgo is a household and trickster spirit of Galician and wider Iberian folklore, a small mischievous shapeshifter that haunts barns, kitchens, and settlements, stealing food and playing pranks on residents. Legends recount how it may be expelled or tamed by outwitting it. It belongs to the family of Iberian domestic goblins associated with rural life.
source: Spanish folk belief and ethnographic records of regional traditions (Galician, Asturian, Catalan)
research_notes: Matches input appearance (deceiving, shapeshifting, mischievous), behavior, habitat (human dwellings, barns, settlements), and cultural significance (Galician trickster). Related to Asturian trasgu and other Iberian household goblins.

description: Xanas are water spirits of Asturian folklore, beautiful young women who dwell in springs, rivers, and caves (cuevas de xanas), often combing their long hair by the water and offering gifts or trials to passersby. Documented by Ramón Menéndez Pidal, the tradition is connected to pre-Roman Celtic belief and the cult of Diana; the name derives from Diana or Jana.
source: Asturian folklore; Xanas are water nymphs associated with caves and springs
research_notes: Matches input: documented by Menéndez Pidal, linked to pre-Roman Celtic belief and the cult of Diana, name from Diana/Jana, habitat of streams, rivers, and xana caves.

description: Xnifs are mischievous imps of Maltese folklore said to live in ruins and abandoned places, causing minor household troubles and pilfering food. They belong to the broader class of Mediterranean household and ruin-dwelling goblins. The belief is recorded in Maltese oral tradition, though documentation is sparse and largely secondary.
source: Maltese folklore — Xnifs goblin documented in Maltese oral tradition
research_notes: Attestation is thin but consistent with the input's cultural significance (Maltese imps, minor household spirits). Source_quality lowered to 'fair' to match the sparse documentation.

description: Mari is the supreme goddess of Basque religion, a powerful spirit associated with caves, mountains, weather, and the cycles of nature. She appears as a beautiful woman or a terrible dragon and may bring blessing or destruction, rewarding respect and punishing violation of her taboos. She is the central figure of Basque mythology, with her consort Sugaar beneath her.
source: Spanish folk belief and ethnographic records of regional traditions (Basque)
research_notes: Matches input appearance (beautiful woman or terrible dragon), behavior (blessing or destruction), habitat (caves and caverns in Basque landscapes), and cultural significance (supreme goddess of Basque religion).

description: El Marraco is the dragon of Lleida in Catalan folklore, depicted as a wingless green dragon with sharp claws and, in older accounts, linked to the ancient Ilergetes, whose chieftains were said to descend from a dragon deity. Today it appears in the city's festive processions (bestiari), preserving a folk memory of pre-Roman Iberian belief within Catholic celebration.
source: Spanish folklore — Marraco dragon documented in Catalan oral tradition
research_notes: Matches input appearance (wingless green dragon with sharp claws), behavior (hoarding, territorial), habitat (Catalan mountains and lairs), and cultural significance (Ilergetes descent tradition, Lleida).

description: Masche are the witches of Piedmontese tradition, women who inherited supernatural powers across generations, able to change into animals, fly, and cast spells. Distinct from Sardinian or Neapolitan witchcraft, their power was held to come from nature rather than the devil. Feared but also consulted for healing, they are remembered in a major festival at Rifreddo.
source: Italian folk belief and regional ethnographic records of local spirits and legends
research_notes: Matches input appearance (shapeshifting into animals, flying, casting spells), behavior, habitat (isolated houses, forests, mountains of Piedmont), and cultural significance (nature-derived powers, Rifreddo festival).

description: The mauve sorcière is a witch figure of French folklore identified by Claude Lecouteux, whose name refers to the purple-tinged assemblies of witches, perhaps tied to the Devil's Sabbath. These gatherings at crossroads and isolated places mark the color mauve as the hue of the witches' supernatural realm. The figure condenses the fear of rural witchcraft and the sabbat in French folk belief.
source: French folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions and regional legends (cf. C. Lecouteux)
research_notes: Matches input: mauve = purple-colored witch gatherings, possibly connected to the Devil's Sabbath; habitat of villages, crossroads, isolated places. Based on Lecouteux's research on French witchcraft.

description: Medusa is the most famous of the three Gorgon sisters of Greek myth, a winged being with living serpents for hair whose gaze turned all who met it to stone. Once a beautiful maiden punished by Athena, she was beheaded by Perseus, and from her neck sprang Pegasus and Chrysaor. Her severed head, the gorgoneion, became an apotropaic emblem on armor and shields.
source: Greek mythology, Hesiod & Homer
research_notes: Matches input appearance (serpents for hair, gaze turns to stone), behavior (Perseus, Pegasus and Chrysaor, petrifying gaze), habitat (cave near the ends of the earth), and cultural significance (gorgoneion as apotropaic symbol).

description: Meigas are the wise women of Galician folklore, healers and practitioners who communicate with nature and the supernatural and who can cure or harm. Unlike the malevolent witch stereotype, they were knowledgeable community figures consulted for healing and divination. The tradition is recorded in Galician oral tradition and remains part of regional identity.
source: Spanish/Galician folklore — Meiga documented in Galician oral tradition
research_notes: Matches input appearance (wise women with power to communicate with nature), behavior (can heal or harm), habitat (Galician communities), and cultural significance (knowledgeable healers, not malevolent witches).

description: The mellified man (mellified mummy) is a legendary remedy from Arabic and Chinese sources, famously recorded by Li Shizhen in the Bencao Gangmu, in which willing elderly men were steeped in honey until their bodies dissolved into a curative confection. Though almost certainly fanciful, the tale circulated along the Silk Road as an emblem of extreme preservation and folk medicine.

description: Melusine is a fresh-water spirit of French folklore, often a woman who becomes a serpent or mermaid below the waist, sometimes winged. In the medieval romance she married Raymondin of Lusignan, provided he never saw her on Saturdays; when he broke the oath she fled as a serpent. She is the legendary ancestress of the Lusignan, Anjou, and Luxembourg dynasties.
source: French folklore; Melusine is a feminine spirit of fresh water in folklore, often a serpent-woman (cf. Wikipedia FR)
research_notes: Verified against the French Wikipedia article on Melusine: freshwater spirit, serpent/fish lower body, wings and two tails, Pressine and Elinas origin tale (Well of Thirst, triplets Melusine/Melior/Palatine), Lusignan/Anjou/Luxembourg descent legends.

description: The Minotaur is a monster of Greek myth, a man with the head and body of a bull, born of Pasiphaë and the Cretan bull and known as Asterion. Confined by Daedalus in the Labyrinth beneath Knossos and fed on human tribute from Athens, it was slain by Theseus with the aid of Ariadne's thread. Its story may encode Minoan bull-cult and the palace's intricate architecture.
source: Greek mythology, Hesiod & Homer (cf. Britannica, Wikipedia)
research_notes: Verified against Britannica and Wikipedia: Pasiphae + Poseidon's white bull, Labyrinth by Daedalus, Theseus + Ariadne, name Asterion. Matches input appearance, behavior, habitat (Labyrinth of Knossos), and cultural significance.

description: Moura encantadas are enchanted women of Portuguese folklore bound to megalithic monuments, who appear as beauties with golden or black hair combing their tresses and singing beside springs, dolmens, and cromlechs. They guard hidden treasures and may reward or punish those who encounter them. Documented by José Leite de Vasconcelos, these beliefs have guided archaeologists to ancient sites.
source: Portuguese folklore; the Moura Encantada is a supernatural female spirit guarding treasures
research_notes: Matches input appearance (beautiful women with golden/black hair, singing by springs), behavior, habitat (dolmens, cromlechs, ancient stone sites), and cultural significance (documented by Leite de Vasconcelos; used by archaeologists to locate sites).

description: The lobisomem is the Portuguese werewolf, a person cursed to run out a fado (spell) at night as an animal — in the north a horse, in the south a donkey, dog, or pig. Seventh consecutive sons, children of incest, and the unbaptized were destined for the curse, broken only by drawing the werewolf's blood with steel. The belief is documented in Portugal and carried to Brazil.

research_notes: Verified via Springer chapter on Portuguese werewolf belief narratives and Rodney Gallop (1936): lobisomem as horse (north) / donkey or dog (south), seventh-child curse, blood-drawing cure, protective baptismal names (Adam, Bento, etc.). description: The lobisón is the werewolf of Galician folklore, the regional form of the Iberian lobishome. Its most famous association is Manuel Blanco Romasanta, a nineteenth-century Galician serial killer tried in 1853, who claimed he transformed into a wolf under a curse — a plea that entered Spanish legal and folkloric history. The legend encodes the fear of the man-beast in rural Galicia.

research_notes: Distinct from the South American lobizón/lobisón. Matches input cultural significance (famous legal case, Manuel Blanco Romasanta, the 'werewolf of Allariz'). Input appearance/behavior were template placeholders; replaced with the attested Galician tradition.

description: The loupo is the werewolf of Occitan and Alpine French tradition, a loup-garou variant recorded in Savoie and Dauphiné, where belief in human-wolf metamorphosis was widespread. Local accounts describe men who changed shape under a curse and roamed the mountains at night, illustrating pre-Christian shapeshifting belief in southern France, distinct from the northern loup-garou.

description: Il lupo mannaro is the Italian werewolf, a person cursed or voluntarily transformed into a wolf to hunt humans, attested since antiquity as lupus hominarius and versipellis ('skin-changer'). Folk tradition distinguished induced, voluntary, and spontaneous lycanthropy, with regional names like lupo menaro and lupunaru. In Basilicata, children born on Christmas night were said to become wolves.

description: Undines are water elementals introduced by Paracelsus in A Book on Nymphs (1566), named from Latin unda ('wave') and classed among the four elemental spirits alongside gnomes, sylphs, and salamanders. Said to lack an immortal soul, they could gain one by marrying a mortal — a motif that inspired Friedrich de la Motte Fouqué's novella Undine (1811) and later the Little Mermaid tradition.

research_notes: Verified against Wikipedia: Paracelsus, Book on Nymphs 1566, elemental classification, Latin unda, Fouqué 1811 novella, Little Mermaid link. Matches input appearance (female water spirit of fountains, springs, forest pools), behavior, and cultural significance.

description: The griffin (gryps) is a Greek and Near Eastern hybrid of lion and eagle, combining the king of beasts with the king of birds. Aristeas, Herodotus, and Pliny describe it guarding Scythian gold against the one-eyed Arimaspians; scholars link the legend to Protoceratops fossils near Central Asian gold. It became heraldry’s emblem of guardianship and divine power.
source: Greek mythology, Hesiod & Homer (cf. Wikipedia, theoi.com, Britannica)
research_notes: Verified against Wikipedia and theoi.com: lion body, eagle head and wings, Aristeas/Herodotus/Aeschylus/Pliny accounts, Arimaspian gold wars, Adrienne Mayor's Protoceratops theory, heraldic use. Matches the input's detailed appearance and behavior.

description: Fairies are supernatural beings of European folk belief, spanning Celtic (aes sídhe, Tuatha Dé Danann), Germanic (elves, dwarves), Slavic, and Romance traditions. The term derives from Old French faerie, from fae, from Latin fata ('fate'). Origins include demoted angels, spirits of the dead, nature spirits, or a hidden earlier race; in tales they act as helpers, abductors, or amoral tricksters.

description: In Italian folklore the fata is a fairy or fate-like woman whose name descends from Latin fata, the goddesses of destiny, and who appears in the Pentamerone and other collections as a magical benefactress or enchantress. Italian fairies blend the classical Parcae with medieval enchantresses such as Morgan le Fay, and regional figures from the Befana to water spirits are classed among them.

description: In French tradition the fée is a supernatural woman who grants gifts to newborns and shapes the destiny of mortals, dwelling in forests, springs, and castles of the Otherworld. Two archetypes dominate medieval literature: the fairy godmother and the fairy lover (Morgane, Viviane, Melusine). Regional forms such as the dames blanches and the fées des houles preserve older, more ambivalent beliefs.
source: France mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections (cf. Harf-Lancner; Sébillot; Wikipedia FR)
